newsitem.title: PORTUGAL: FORECAST - Iberian bonds eye EMU, CPI developments.
newsitem.headline: FORECAST - Iberian bonds eye EMU, CPI developments.

text.p: Iberian bonds should track core European markets closely over the coming week, with some room for narrowing of the spread with the Bunds, provided there are no single currency shocks, analysts said on Friday.
They said the market would be looking for the meeting of European Union finance ministers, Ecofin, on Sunday and Monday to reaffirm the determination to launch the single currency as planned in 1999.
Any hint of trouble, however, could alter the market stance dramatically, sending the spreads with the 10-year Bunds sharply wider, they added.

Analysts expect both Spain and Portugal to announce that May was another good month on the inflation front, with the Spanish consumer price index (CPI) due on June 13 and the Portuguese a few days later.

The Ecofin will discuss the Stability Pact, which the new leftwing government in France said during the election campaign it wanted reviewed. European Union heads of government will meet for a summit on June 16 and 17.
The spreads between the Bonos and the (Portuguese) OT and the 10-year Bunds are 76 and 68 basis points, respectively, compared with historic lows of 64 and 50 basis points touched two weeks ago.

"It should be a volatile week. Until we know how the issue of the euro (single currency) is going to be resolved, Spain and Portugal are going to following the hard core market (Bund)," said analyst Henrik Lumholdt of Bank of America in Madrid.
Nuno Godinho of Deutsche Morgam Grenfell in Lisbon said he doubted that the Stability Pact would be put in doubt and that confidence that the euro will be launched on time could grow.
"It is not impossible that the spreads (with the Bunds) move back closer to the levels of two weeks ago," he said.
"My feeling is that there will be no bad news next week, despite that fact that it could be volatile," said Luis Pina of Banco ESSI in Lisbon.
If, however, there were any unfavourable announcements about the euro, then the spreads could widen to 90-95 basis points in the case of Spain and 80-85 in the case of Portugal, analysts said.

"Much is going to depend on Germany, which has its own problems, whether it is going to take a cooperative line with the new French government or be intransigent," said Valentim Fernandez of Credit Lionnais in Madrid.
Analysts said that good inflation numbers in both countries would give additional support to the short end and steepen the yield curve.
"The year-on-year rate (in Spain in May) could be 1.5 percent and the Bank of Spain could greet it with a cut of 25 basis points on (June) 16," said Lumholdt.
Inflation in Portugal was seen between 1.5 and 1.7 percent which could allow the central bank there to also cut rates, analysts said.

"If the market continues to bet on the single currency in 1999, with Spain and Portugal inside, the curve could steepen, with the two year (April 1999) Bono yield going to 4.90 percent (from 5.09 percent at present)," said Valentin Fernandez.
